Tree-Ring Growth Response of Netleaf Hackberry (Celtis reticulata) to Evapotranspiration and Soil Moisture on the Lower Salmon River, Idaho

Swabhiman Reule

2026-05-07

Introduction

Tree-ring width indices (RWI) are widely used to reconstruct past climate variability, with most studies focusing on precipitation and drought-related variables (Fritts, 1976; Cook & Kairiukstis, 1990). Evapotranspiration (ET), which represents atmospheric water demand, has been less explored in dendroclimatology due to its indirect relationship with plant-available water. Netleaf Hackberry (Celtis reticulata), a slow-growing, long-lived drought-tolerant tree reaching its northern limit in Idaho (DeBolt & McCune, 1995), provides a unique opportunity to evaluate growth sensitivity to water availability along the Lower Salmon River Canyon. Despite its ecological importance, Celtis reticulata has received very little dendrochronological attention, making this one of the first studies of its climate-growth relationships. This study evaluates the relationship between ET and root zone soil moisture (SMrz) from GLEAM v4.2a (Martens et al., 2017) and Hackberry radial growth across 14 sites to assess which variable better predicts interannual growth variability.

Study Area

The study was conducted along the Lower Salmon River Canyon in north-central Idaho, USA. The Salmon River is a major tributary of the Snake River and flows through a deeply incised canyon characterized by steep rocky slopes, semi-arid climate, and hot dry summers. The study area spans approximately 60 km along the river corridor, with sampling sites distributed across a range of topographic positions including river terraces, rocky draws, and canyon slopes. Netleaf Hackberry (Celtis reticulata) is a dominant woody species at many sites within this canyon system, occurring on south-facing rocky slopes and riparian terraces along the river.

The interactive map below shows the spatial distribution of all 14 sampling sites along the Lower Salmon River Canyon. Click on any site to see its name. Use the layer control to switch between Topo Map, Satellite, and Light base maps.

Objectives

  1. Quantify the correlation between tree-ring width index (RWI) and monthly ET and SMrz across 14 sites during the growing season (May–September, 1980–2023)
  2. Determine which climate variable ET or SMrz is a stronger predictor of Hackberry radial growth
  3. Identify the most critical growing season month for Hackberry climate sensitivity
  4. Map the spatial distribution of climate-growth correlation strength across all 14 sites
  5. Test whether sites with similar climate-growth responses are spatially clustered using spatial autocorrelation analysis

Methodology

Tree-Ring Data Collection

Increment cores were collected from 169 Netleaf Hackberry (Celtis reticulata) trees across 14 sites along the Lower Salmon River, Idaho. Two cores per tree were extracted at approximately 20 cm above the ground surface due to the relatively short stature of Hackberry trees in this region. In the laboratory, cores were mounted on wooden supports and progressively sanded with increasingly fine sandpaper to clearly reveal annual ring boundaries. Ring widths were measured to the nearest 0.001 mm using the CooRecorder program. Individual ring-width series were crossdated to ensure accurate year assignment.

Chronology Development

Ring-width series were detrended using a modified negative exponential function to remove biological growth trends related to tree age and size. This standardization process produces the Ring Width Index (RWI), where values greater than 1.0 indicate above-average growth years and values less than 1.0 indicate below-average growth years. Chronologies were developed for each site using the dplR package (Bunn, 2008) in R, with the overlap period for climate analysis being 1980–2023 (n = 44 years) based on the availability of GLEAM climate data.

Detrend RWL to CRN

library(dplR)
library(ncdf4)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(sf)
library(spdep)
library(gstat)
library(leaflet)
library(htmltools)
library(htmlwidgets)

cat("✓ All packages loaded!\n")
## ✓ All packages loaded!
crn_dir   <- "C:/Hackberry_Spatial_AA/Chronologies"
rwl_files <- list.files(crn_dir, pattern = "\\.rwl$",
                        full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)

cat("RWL files found:", length(rwl_files), "\n\n")
## RWL files found: 14
for (f in rwl_files) {
  site_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  cat("Processing:", site_name, "... ")
  rwl <- read.rwl(f)
  rwi <- detrend(rwl = rwl, method = "ModNegExp")
  crn <- chron(rwi, prefix = site_name)
  crn_out <- file.path(crn_dir, paste0(site_name, ".crn"))
  write.crn(crn, crn_out)
  cat("✓\n")
}

Climate Data - GLEAM v4.2a

Monthly evapotranspiration (ET) and root zone soil moisture (SMrz) were obtained from the GLEAM v4.2a dataset (Martens et al., 2017). GLEAM stands for Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model — a satellite-based global model that estimates actual evapotranspiration and root zone soil moisture at a spatial resolution of 0.1° (~10 km) on a monthly basis from 1980 to present. ET is expressed in mm/month representing the total water transferred from land to atmosphere. SMrz is expressed in volumetric water content (m³/m³) representing the actual water stored in the root zone soil layer. Climate data were extracted for the study site coordinates (Lat: 45.6939°N, Lon: -116.3106°W) from 45 annual NetCDF files for each variable using the nearest grid cell.

Extract ET

site_lon <- -116.3106
site_lat <-  45.6939

et_dir   <- "C:/Hackberry_Spatial_AA/ET"
nc_files <- list.files(et_dir, pattern = "\\.nc$",
                       full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)

cat("ET NC files found:", length(nc_files), "\n")
## ET NC files found: 45
et_list <- list()
for (f in nc_files) {
  nc         <- nc_open(f)
  lon_vals   <- ncvar_get(nc, "lon")
  lat_vals   <- ncvar_get(nc, "lat")
  time_raw   <- ncvar_get(nc, "time")
  time_units <- ncatt_get(nc, "time", "units")$value
  lon_idx    <- which.min(abs(lon_vals - site_lon))
  lat_idx    <- which.min(abs(lat_vals - site_lat))
  vals       <- ncvar_get(nc, "E",
                          start = c(lon_idx, lat_idx, 1),
                          count = c(1, 1, -1))
  fv <- ncatt_get(nc, "E", "_FillValue")$value
  if (!is.logical(fv)) vals[vals == fv] <- NA
  origin_date <- as.Date(trimws(sub(" 00:00:00", "",
                  sub("days since ", "", time_units))))
  dates <- origin_date + time_raw
  et_list[[basename(f)]] <- data.frame(
    date  = as.Date(dates),
    year  = year(dates),
    month = month(dates),
    ET    = as.numeric(vals)
  )
  nc_close(nc)
}

et_ts <- bind_rows(et_list) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  distinct(date, .keep_all = TRUE)

et_wide <- et_ts %>%
  filter(year >= 1980 & year <= 2024) %>%
  select(year, month, ET) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from  = month,
              values_from = ET) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("ET_", month.abb[as.integer(.)]), -year)

## Total months: 540
cat("ET range    : min =", round(min(et_ts$ET, na.rm=TRUE), 2),
    "| max =", round(max(et_ts$ET, na.rm=TRUE), 2), "mm/month\n")

Statistical Techniques

Five statistical techniques were used in this study to analyze the climate-growth relationships between Hackberry tree-ring growth and the climate variables ET and SMrz.

1. Pearson Correlation

Pearson correlation coefficient (r) measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables in this case between RWI and monthly ET or SMrz. The r value ranges from -1 to +1, where values close to +1 indicate a strong positive relationship, values close to -1 indicate a strong negative relationship, and values near 0 indicate no relationship. Statistical significance was assessed at p < 0.05 with a critical r value of 0.294 (n = 44 years). This technique is useful because it directly quantifies how strongly each month’s ET or SMrz predicts tree growth across all 14 sites.

2. Linear Regression

Simple linear regression (RWI ~ ET or RWI ~ SMrz) was used to quantify the proportion of variance in tree-ring growth explained by each climate variable (R²). While Pearson correlation shows the strength of the relationship, R² tells us how much of the variation in tree growth can be predicted by the climate variable. For example, R² = 0.42 means that 42% of the year-to-year variation in ring width is explained by soil moisture. This allows direct comparison of the predictive power of ET versus SMrz across all 14 sites.

3. Seasonal Window Analysis

Seasonal window analysis tests all possible combinations of consecutive growing season months (May through September) to identify the optimal seasonal window the combination of months that produces the strongest climate-growth correlation at each site. This technique is standard in dendroclimatology and helps identify the critical period when climate most strongly controls tree growth. For example, if August alone produces the highest correlation, that tells us late summer water availability is the most important period for Hackberry growth.

4. Moran’s I Spatial Autocorrelation

Moran’s I is a statistical measure of spatial autocorrelation. It tests whether sites with similar climate-growth response values are spatially clustered or randomly distributed across the landscape. A significant positive Moran’s I (p < 0.05) indicates that nearby sites respond similarly to ET or SMrz. Suggesting that local landscape factors such as topographic position or proximity to the river drive spatial patterns in climate sensitivity. A non-significant result indicates that sensitivity is randomly distributed with no spatial pattern.

5. IDW Interpolation

Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation is a spatial technique that creates a continuous surface of estimated values from a set of known point measurements. It works by weighting nearby points more heavily than distant points when estimating values at unsampled locations. In this study IDW was applied to the site-level Pearson correlation coefficients to produce a continuous raster surface showing the spatial gradient of ET and SMrz climate sensitivity across the Lower Salmon River study area beyond the 14 sampled locations.

Results

Annual Time Series - ET and SMrz Trends (1980–2024)

Before analyzing climate-growth relationships, we first examined the long-term trends in ET and SMrz at the study site. Annual total ET and annual mean SMrz were calculated for each year from 1980 to 2024. A linear trend line was fitted to each time series to identify directional changes over the study period.

# ET annual total
et_annual <- et_ts %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(annual_ET = sum(ET, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups   = "drop")

ggplot(et_annual, aes(x = year, y = annual_ET)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              color = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title    = "Annual Total ET — Lower Salmon River",
       subtitle = "GLEAM v4.2a | 1980–2024",
       x = "Year", y = "Annual ET (mm/year)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text  = element_text(size = 12, color = "black",
                                  face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

# SMrz annual mean
sm_annual <- sm_ts %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(annual_SM = mean(SM, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups   = "drop")

ggplot(sm_annual, aes(x = year, y = annual_SM)) +
  geom_line(color = "sienna", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              color = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title    = "Annual Mean SMrz — Lower Salmon River",
       subtitle = "GLEAM v4.2a | 1980–2024",
       x = "Year", y = "Annual Mean SMrz (m³/m³)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text  = element_text(size = 12, color = "black",
                                  face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Pearson Correlation and Linear Regression - ET vs RWI

Pearson correlation and linear regression were used to quantify the relationship between monthly ET and Hackberry ring width index (RWI) during the growing season (May–September) at all 14 sites for the overlap period 1980–2023.

growing_months      <- 5:9
growing_month_names <- month.abb[growing_months]

gs_results <- list()

for (i in seq_along(crn_files)) {
  site    <- site_names[i]
  crn_tmp <- dplR::read.crn(crn_files[i])
  yrs     <- as.integer(rownames(crn_tmp))
  rwi     <- crn_tmp[, 1]
  overlap <- intersect(yrs, et_wide$year)
  if (length(overlap) < 20) next
  rwi_ov  <- rwi[yrs %in% overlap]
  et_ov   <- et_wide %>% filter(year %in% overlap)

  for (m in growing_months) {
    col    <- paste0("ET_", month.abb[m])
    et_val <- et_ov[[col]]
    valid  <- !is.na(et_val) & !is.na(rwi_ov)
    if (sum(valid) < 10) next
    ct  <- cor.test(rwi_ov[valid], et_val[valid],
                    method = "pearson")
    mod <- lm(rwi_ov[valid] ~ et_val[valid])
    gs_results[[paste(site, m, sep = "_")]] <- data.frame(
      site        = site,
      month_name  = month.abb[m],
      month_num   = m,
      r           = round(ct$estimate, 2),
      r2          = round(summary(mod)$r.squared, 3),
      p_cor       = ct$p.value,
      significant = ifelse(ct$p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
}

gs_overall <- gs_results_df %>%
  group_by(site) %>%
  summarise(
    best_r     = round(r[which.min(p_cor)], 2),
    best_p_raw = min(p_cor),
    best_month = as.character(month_name[which.min(p_cor)]),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    sig_label    = case_when(
      best_p_raw < 0.001 ~ "***",
      best_p_raw < 0.01  ~ "**",
      best_p_raw < 0.05  ~ "*",
      TRUE               ~ "ns"),
    best_p_label = case_when(
      best_p_raw < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
      TRUE ~ paste0("=", sprintf("%.4f", best_p_raw))),
    panel_label  = paste0(site, "\n", best_month,
                          " r=", best_r,
                          " p",  best_p_label,
                          " ",   sig_label)
  )

gs_plot_df <- gs_results_df %>%
  left_join(gs_overall %>%
              select(site, panel_label), by = "site")

p1 <- ggplot(gs_plot_df,
       aes(x = month_name, y = r, group = 1)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = r),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(color = significant, size = significant)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept =  0.294, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "red", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -0.294, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "red", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Yes" = "darkred",
                                "No"  = "steelblue")) +
  scale_size_manual(values  = c("Yes" = 4, "No" = 2.5)) +

Pearson Correlation and Linear Regression - SMrz vs RWI

Pearson correlation and linear regression were used to quantify the relationship between monthly SMrz and Hackberry ring width index (RWI) during the growing season (May–September) at all 14 sites for the overlap period 1980–2023.

sm_results <- list()

for (i in seq_along(crn_files)) {
  site    <- site_names[i]
  crn_tmp <- dplR::read.crn(crn_files[i])
  yrs     <- as.integer(rownames(crn_tmp))
  rwi     <- crn_tmp[, 1]
  overlap <- intersect(yrs, sm_wide$year)
  if (length(overlap) < 20) next
  rwi_ov  <- rwi[yrs %in% overlap]
  sm_ov   <- sm_wide %>% filter(year %in% overlap)

  for (m in growing_months) {
    col    <- paste0("SM_", month.abb[m])
    sm_val <- sm_ov[[col]]
    valid  <- !is.na(sm_val) & !is.na(rwi_ov)
    if (sum(valid) < 10) next
    ct  <- cor.test(rwi_ov[valid], sm_val[valid],
                    method = "pearson")
    mod <- lm(rwi_ov[valid] ~ sm_val[valid])
    sm_results[[paste(site, m, sep = "_")]] <- data.frame(
      site        = site,
      month_name  = month.abb[m],
      month_num   = m,
      r           = round(ct$estimate, 2),
      r2          = round(summary(mod)$r.squared, 3),
      p_cor       = ct$p.value,
      significant = ifelse(ct$p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
}

Moran’s I — Spatial Autocorrelation

Moran’s I tests whether sites with similar climate-growth response values are spatially clustered or randomly distributed along the river corridor. Sites were connected using k-nearest neighbors (k = 4) to define the spatial neighborhood structure. A significant positive Moran’s I (p < 0.05) indicates that nearby sites respond similarly to ET or SMrz.

site_coords <- data.frame(
  site = c("PBC", "Site013", "Site017", "Site028",
           "Site036", "Site037", "Site038", "Site041",
           "Site045", "Site050", "Site200", "Site212",
           "Site232", "Site502"),
  lon  = c(-116.3299, -116.4046, -116.7040, -116.2923,
           -116.3655, -116.3667, -116.4094, -116.3722,
           -116.3315, -116.3003, -116.3227, -116.4198,
           -116.3305, -116.4164),
  lat  = c(45.8970, 45.9028, 45.9988, 45.6456,
           45.8997, 45.9027, 45.9119, 45.8990,
           45.8907, 45.6264, 45.7619, 45.9161,
           45.4109, 45.9053)
) %>%
  left_join(
    gs_results_df %>%
      group_by(site) %>%
      summarise(
        ET_r   = round(r[which.min(p_cor)], 3),
        ET_sig = ifelse(min(p_cor) < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
        .groups = "drop"),
    by = "site") %>%
  left_join(
    sm_results_df %>%
      group_by(site) %>%
      summarise(
        SM_r   = round(r[which.min(p_cor)], 3),
        SM_sig = ifelse(min(p_cor) < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
        .groups = "drop"),
    by = "site")

# Convert to sf
sites_sf <- st_as_sf(site_coords,
                     coords = c("lon", "lat"),
                     crs    = 4326)

# Spatial weights — k=4 nearest neighbors
coords_mat <- st_coordinates(sites_sf)
knn        <- knearneigh(coords_mat, k = 4)
nb         <- knn2nb(knn)
lw         <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

cat("✓ Spatial weights ready!\n")
## ✓ Spatial weights ready!
cat("Sites:", length(nb), "| k-nearest neighbors: 4\n")
## Sites: 14 | k-nearest neighbors: 4
# Moran's I — ET
moran_et <- moran.test(sites_sf$ET_r, lw,
                        randomisation = TRUE)

# Moran's I — SMrz
moran_sm <- moran.test(sites_sf$SM_r, lw,
                        randomisation = TRUE)

cat("=== MORAN'S I RESULTS ===\n\n")
## === MORAN'S I RESULTS ===
cat("--- ET Climate-Growth Response ---\n")
## --- ET Climate-Growth Response ---
cat("Moran's I statistic:", round(moran_et$estimate[1], 4), "\n")
## Moran's I statistic: -0.1463
cat("Expected value:     ", round(moran_et$estimate[2], 4), "\n")
## Expected value:      -0.0769
cat("p-value:            ", round(moran_et$p.value,     4), "\n")
## p-value:             0.6911
cat("Interpretation:     ",
    ifelse(moran_et$p.value < 0.05,
           ifelse(moran_et$estimate[1] > 0,
                  "SIGNIFICANT CLUSTERING",
                  "SIGNIFICANT DISPERSION"),
           "NOT SIGNIFICANT — Random distribution"), "\n\n")
## Interpretation:      NOT SIGNIFICANT — Random distribution
cat("--- SMrz Climate-Growth Response ---\n")
## --- SMrz Climate-Growth Response ---
cat("Moran's I statistic:", round(moran_sm$estimate[1], 4), "\n")
## Moran's I statistic: 0.013
cat("Expected value:     ", round(moran_sm$estimate[2], 4), "\n")
## Expected value:      -0.0769
cat("p-value:            ", round(moran_sm$p.value,     4), "\n")
## p-value:             0.2496
cat("Interpretation:     ",
    ifelse(moran_sm$p.value < 0.05,
           ifelse(moran_sm$estimate[1] > 0,
                  "SIGNIFICANT CLUSTERING",
                  "SIGNIFICANT DISPERSION"),
           "NOT SIGNIFICANT — Random distribution"), "\n")
## Interpretation:      NOT SIGNIFICANT — Random distribution
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

moran.plot(sites_sf$ET_r, lw,
           main = "Moran's I: ET Response",
           xlab = "ET Pearson r (site)",
           ylab = "Spatially Lagged ET r",
           pch  = 16, col = "steelblue",
           cex  = 1.5)
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
mtext(paste0("I = ", round(moran_et$estimate[1], 3),
             " | p = ", round(moran_et$p.value, 4)),
      side = 3, line = 0.3, cex = 0.9, font = 2)

moran.plot(sites_sf$SM_r, lw,
           main = "Moran's I: SMrz Response",
           xlab = "SMrz Pearson r (site)",
           ylab = "Spatially Lagged SMrz r",
           pch  = 16, col = "sienna",
           cex  = 1.5)
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
mtext(paste0("I = ", round(moran_sm$estimate[1], 3),
             " | p = ", round(moran_sm$p.value, 4)),
      side = 3, line = 0.3, cex = 0.9, font = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The Moran’s I scatter plot shows the relationship between each site’s climate-growth correlation value and the average value of its neighboring sites. Points in the upper-right and lower-left quadrants indicate spatial clustering. A positive significant result would mean that nearby sites along the Lower Salmon River tend to respond similarly to ET or SMrz, suggesting that landscape position drives spatial variation in Hackberry climate sensitivity.

IDW Interpolation - Spatial Sensitivity Surface

Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation was used to create continuous spatial surfaces of ET and SMrz climate sensitivity from the 14 sampling point locations. This reveals the spatial gradient of climate-growth response across the Lower Salmon River study area beyond the 14 sampled points.

# Project to UTM Zone 11N
sites_proj <- st_transform(sites_sf, crs = 32611)

# Create interpolation grid
bbox   <- st_bbox(sites_proj)
buffer <- 8000

grid_points <- expand.grid(
  x = seq(bbox["xmin"] - buffer,
           bbox["xmax"] + buffer, by = 1500),
  y = seq(bbox["ymin"] - buffer,
           bbox["ymax"] + buffer, by = 1500)
)

grid_sf <- st_as_sf(grid_points,
                    coords = c("x", "y"),
                    crs    = 32611)

cat("✓ Interpolation grid ready!\n")
## ✓ Interpolation grid ready!
cat("Grid points:", nrow(grid_sf), "\n")
## Grid points: 1815
cat("Resolution: 1500 m\n")
## Resolution: 1500 m
idw_et <- idw(formula   = ET_r ~ 1,
              locations = sites_proj,
              newdata   = grid_sf,
              idp       = 2)
## [inverse distance weighted interpolation]
idw_et_df <- data.frame(
  x    = st_coordinates(grid_sf)[, 1],
  y    = st_coordinates(grid_sf)[, 2],
  pred = idw_et$var1.pred
)

sites_et_xy <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(sites_proj)) %>%
  mutate(site   = sites_proj$site,

    low      = "#fdf5e6",
    mid      = "#e59866",
    high     = "#6e2c00",
    midpoint = median(idw_sm_df$pred),
    name     = "SMrz r value"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = site_colors,
    name   = "Site"
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("Yes" = 17,   # ← triangle
               "No"  = 16),  # ← circle
    name   = "Significant\n(p<0.05)",
    labels = c("Yes" = "Yes ▲",
               "No"  = "No ●")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure 5b: IDW Interpolation — SMrz Climate-Growth Sensitivity",
    subtitle = "Dark brown = stronger SMrz response | ▲ = significant (p<0.05) | ● = not significant",
    x        = "Easting (m)",
    y        = "Northing (m)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text       = element_text(size = 9, color = "black",
                                   face = "bold"),
    axis.title      = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.text     = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
    legend.title    = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
  )

The IDW interpolation maps reveal the spatial gradient of climate sensitivity across the Lower Salmon River study area. Darker areas indicate locations where tree growth is more strongly correlated with ET or SMrz. The SMrz sensitivity surface (Figure 5b) shows stronger and more widespread signals compared to the ET surface (Figure 5a), visually confirming that soil moisture is the more important driver of Hackberry growth across the landscape.

Discussion

Root zone soil moisture (SMrz) was identified as the primary driver of Hackberry radial growth, showing significant positive correlations at 8 of 14 sites and explaining greater variance (R² = 0.421) than ET (R² = 0.273). ET was significant at 6 of 14 sites with August emerging as the most critical growth month across all sites. The consistent positive direction of SMrz-growth relationships indicates that water supply rather than atmospheric demand controls interannual growth variability in Hackberry at this riparian location.

The increasing trend in growing season ET observed after 2010, combined with strong soil moisture-growth relationships suggests that Hackberry populations along the Lower Salmon River face increasing water stress under future climate warming. If soil moisture availability declines while atmospheric demand increases, sustained below-average growth or population decline may occur along this semi-arid river corridor.

The Moran’s I spatial autocorrelation analysis tested whether nearby sites along the river respond similarly to ET and SMrz. The IDW interpolation maps reveal where along the river corridor Hackberry is most sensitive to hydroclimate variability providing a spatial picture of climate sensitivity that goes beyond the 14 individual point measurements.

Conclusion

  • SMrz is the primary driver of Hackberry radial growth significant at 8 of 14 sites (max R² = 0.421)
  • ET was significant at 6 of 14 sites (max R² = 0.273) not the primary driver
  • August is the most critical growing season month for both variables
  • Site232 showed the strongest climate signal SMrz r = 0.66, p < 0.001
  • ET has been increasing since 2010 rising atmospheric water demand
  • Moran’s I tested spatial clustering of climate sensitivity along the river corridor
  • IDW interpolation revealed the spatial gradient of ET and SMrz sensitivity
  • Hackberry growth is vulnerable to future drought as soil moisture declines

Future Work

1. Extend climate-growth analysis using pre-1980 climate records (PRISM, CRU) to utilize the full chronology length (1830–2023) and analyze more years of growth response instead of the current 44-year overlap period.

2. Expand tree-ring sampling to 30–50 sites across Idaho to capture regional spatial patterns in Hackberry climate sensitivity and develop statewide climate-growth models for conservation planning.

3. Integrate USGS Salmon River streamflow data to examine hydrological controls on riparian tree growth and reconstruct historical discharge variability from Hackberry chronologies.
